blocks.content: Modules Six and Seven answered how a request finds its way to a container. This module answers a quieter but equally important question: once that container is running, where does it actually get the settings it needs to behave correctly?
ConfigMap, Given Its Own Full Depth
blocks.text: ConfigMap, Given Its Own Full Depth

blocks.content: A ConfigMap is a Kubernetes object that stores non sensitive configuration data as a set of key value pairs, kept entirely separate from the container image and from the Pod spec that references it.

This separation means the exact same container image, built once and pushed to a registry, can be deployed unchanged across development, staging, and production, with each environment supplying its own distinct ConfigMap holding environment specific values.

A ConfigMap can hold simple string values, such as a log level or a feature flag, or entire configuration files, such as a full application config in JSON, YAML, or any other text format the application expects to read.

Like every other object covered throughout this course, a ConfigMap is created declaratively through a YAML manifest and stored in etcd, fully version controlled and fully reviewable through the exact same GitOps workflows already used for Deployments and Services.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731597123-141362194.png
blocks.alt: ConfigMap given its own full depth

blocks.content: Decoupling Configuration From the Image Itself
blocks.text: Decoupling Configuration From the Image Itself

blocks.content: Before ConfigMap, and still in many non Kubernetes systems today, configuration is frequently baked directly into a container image, meaning a change to a single setting, such as a log level, requires rebuilding, retagging, and redeploying the entire image.

A ConfigMap eliminates this coupling entirely. The image contains only the application code, and the ConfigMap, referenced by the Pod spec, supplies every environment specific value the application needs at the moment it actually starts.

This means promoting an application from staging to production becomes a matter of deploying the exact same, already tested image, paired with a different, production specific ConfigMap, rather than rebuilding anything at all.

This decoupling is one of the most immediately practical benefits Kubernetes offers over earlier deployment approaches, and it is the foundational idea every other topic in this module builds directly on top of.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731599225-899357527.png
blocks.alt: A configuration value stored separately from the container image

blocks.content: A Real ConfigMap Example

Consider an application that reads a log level and a feature flag at startup, both values that reasonably differ between a noisy, permissive development environment and a quiet, conservative production environment.

A ConfigMap named app-config holds two keys, LOG_LEVEL and FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT, with development's ConfigMap setting LOG_LEVEL to debug and the feature flag to true, while production's ConfigMap sets LOG_LEVEL to warn and the flag to false.

The application's own Deployment manifest, identical across both environments, simply references a ConfigMap named app-config, with only the ConfigMap's actual content differing between the two environments' own separate manifests.

Changing the feature flag for production, to gradually roll out the new checkout flow, becomes a one line ConfigMap edit and a Pod restart, with zero changes required to the application image or the Deployment manifest itself.

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "warn"
  FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT: "false"

code.content:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "warn"
  FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT: "false"

codes.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "warn"
  FEATURE_NEW_CHECKOUT: "false"

blocks.content: Recap: Why Images Should Stay Environment Agnostic
blocks.text: Recap: Why Images Should Stay Environment Agnostic

blocks.content: Throughout this course, container images have consistently been treated as immutable, versioned artifacts, built once and promoted unchanged through environments, exactly the pattern already established for Deployment rollouts and rollbacks in earlier modules.

A container image that embeds environment specific configuration directly breaks this promise, since the artifact tested in staging is no longer, strictly speaking, the exact same artifact running in production, undermining the entire point of that promotion pattern.

ConfigMap is the concrete mechanism that keeps this promise intact for configuration data specifically, letting the image remain a pure, environment agnostic artifact while the ConfigMap supplies whatever varies from one environment to the next.

Recognizing this connection ties ConfigMap directly back into the broader deployment discipline already established earlier in this course, rather than treating it as an isolated, standalone feature introduced for the first time in this module.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731602706-173967727.png
blocks.alt: Recap of container images remaining environment agnostic

blocks.content: Three Ways a Pod Can Consume a ConfigMap
blocks.text: Three Ways a Pod Can Consume a ConfigMap

blocks.content: A ConfigMap's data can be delivered into a container as environment variables, with each key becoming a distinct environment variable the application reads directly, covered in its own full dedicated depth two topics from now.

A ConfigMap's data can also be mounted as files inside the container's filesystem, with each key becoming a separate file and its value becoming that file's content, covered in its own full dedicated depth later in this module.

A ConfigMap's individual values can also be referenced directly as command line arguments passed to the container's entrypoint, useful for applications configured primarily through command line flags rather than environment variables or config files.

Choosing the right consumption method for a given application's own configuration style is a genuinely practical skill, and the next several topics in this module each give one of these methods the full depth needed to make that choice confidently.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731604441-389599511.png
blocks.alt: Three ways a Pod can consume a ConfigMap

blocks.content: A Common Mistake: Baking Configuration Into the Image
blocks.text: A Common Mistake: Baking Configuration Into the Image

blocks.content: A common mistake, especially among teams new to Kubernetes or migrating from an older deployment approach, is continuing to bake environment specific configuration directly into the container image, using ConfigMap only for a small subset of settings.

This hybrid approach undermines the exact benefit ConfigMap exists to provide: promoting the same image across environments now requires verifying that the baked in configuration also happens to be correct for the new environment, reintroducing the coupling ConfigMap was meant to eliminate.

The fix is a deliberate, disciplined habit: any value that could plausibly differ between development, staging, and production belongs in a ConfigMap or a Secret, never hardcoded into the application code or baked into the image at build time.

This discipline pays off most visibly the first time an emergency configuration change is needed in production. A ConfigMap edit and a Pod restart take moments; a full image rebuild and redeploy takes considerably longer, precisely when time matters most.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/devops-content-images/1784731605986-2251901.png
blocks.alt: The mistake of baking configuration directly into a container image

blocks.content: Creating a ConfigMap From Files or the Command Line
blocks.text: Creating a ConfigMap From Files or the Command Line

blocks.content: Beyond writing a full YAML manifest by hand, kubectl create configmap can generate a ConfigMap directly from an existing file, a directory of files, or literal key value pairs typed directly on the command line, useful for quick, ad hoc creation.

Creating a ConfigMap from an existing configuration file preserves that file's exact content as a single key's value, which is particularly useful for applications that already read their configuration from one well known file format.

For anything intended to be genuinely reproducible and version controlled, writing the ConfigMap manifest directly as YAML, checked into the same repository as the rest of the application's Kubernetes manifests, remains the strongly recommended approach.

The command line generation approach is best reserved for quick local testing or one time exploration, not as the primary way a team manages configuration for any application intended to run in a real, shared environment.
kubectl create configmap app-config --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=warn --from-file=app.properties
ConfigMap Size and Structural Limits

A ConfigMap has a practical size limit, typically around one megabyte total, imposed by etcd's own object size constraints, which is more than sufficient for the vast majority of configuration data but worth knowing about for unusually large configuration files.

For configuration data that genuinely exceeds this limit, the correct approach is generally splitting it across multiple ConfigMaps by logical grouping, or reconsidering whether that specific data belongs in a ConfigMap at all versus a more purpose built storage mechanism.

A single ConfigMap can hold many distinct keys simultaneously, and there is no requirement that an application's entire configuration live in exactly one ConfigMap. Splitting configuration into several logically grouped ConfigMaps is a common and often clearer practice.

Understanding this limit early prevents a surprising failure mode late in a project's life, where a ConfigMap that started small has grown, key by key, over many months, into something silently approaching this practical size ceiling.

ConfigMaps and Namespace Scoping

A ConfigMap, like a Service, is a namespaced object, meaning it exists within exactly one namespace and can only be directly referenced by Pods within that same namespace, without any special cross namespace configuration.

This scoping is a deliberate, useful boundary: a development namespace's app-config ConfigMap and a production namespace's app-config ConfigMap can share the exact same name without any conflict, since each is scoped entirely to its own namespace.

This is precisely the pattern already demonstrated in this topic's real example, where development and production each have their own distinct ConfigMap, both reasonably named app-config, living safely in their own separate namespaces.

Understanding this namespace scoping is genuinely useful for correctly structuring a multi environment cluster, and it connects directly to the Namespaces and Resource Management module covered later in this course.
Immutable ConfigMaps for Stability and Performance
blocks.text: Immutable ConfigMaps for Stability and Performance

blocks.content: Kubernetes supports marking a ConfigMap as immutable, using a dedicated immutable field set to true, which prevents any further changes to its data after creation, requiring a genuinely new ConfigMap object to be created for any update instead.

This immutability offers two real benefits: it eliminates the entire class of accidental in place edits that could unexpectedly affect every Pod referencing that ConfigMap, and it reduces load on the API server, which no longer needs to watch that object for changes.

The tradeoff is that updating an immutable ConfigMap's data requires creating a new object, typically with a version suffix in its name, and updating every Pod spec that references it to point at the new name instead of the old one.

This pattern is particularly well suited to configuration that genuinely should not change without a deliberate, explicit rollout, treating each new version as a distinct, versioned artifact rather than a value silently mutated in place.

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config-v2
immutable: true
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "warn"

code.content:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config-v2
immutable: true
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "warn"

codes.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: app-config-v2
immutable: true
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: "warn"

blocks.content: ConfigMap Updates and Rollout Coordination

For mutable ConfigMaps consumed as environment variables, a change requires a Pod restart to take effect, exactly as covered in full in the Environment Variables topic later in this module, meaning the update and the rollout are two genuinely separate steps.

For mutable ConfigMaps consumed as mounted volumes, a change propagates to running Pods automatically within roughly a minute, without requiring a restart, exactly as covered in full in the Volume Configuration topic later in this module.

Understanding which consumption method a given application uses is essential before assuming a ConfigMap update has taken effect, since the same edit produces genuinely different observable behavior depending on that one choice made when the Pod spec was written.
This distinction, previewed here, is precisely why both consumption methods receive their own full, dedicated topics later in this module rather than being treated as a minor implementation detail.
ConfigMap and Multi Container Pods

A single ConfigMap can be referenced by multiple containers within the same Pod, or by containers across entirely different Pods and even different Deployments, since a ConfigMap's only real scope boundary is its namespace, not any specific Pod or workload.

This sharing capability is genuinely useful for configuration values common to several related components, such as a shared logging format or a shared feature flag consumed identically by both a main application container and a sidecar container within the same Pod.

Sharing one ConfigMap across many consumers does introduce a coordination consideration: a single update now potentially affects every consumer simultaneously, which can be exactly the intended behavior or a genuine risk depending on how tightly those consumers are meant to move together.

Deciding whether to share one ConfigMap broadly or split configuration into several more narrowly scoped ConfigMaps, one per logical consumer, is a real design choice worth making deliberately rather than defaulting unconsciously to whichever is more convenient at the moment.
Best Practices for ConfigMap

Keep sensitive values, such as passwords, API keys, and tokens, out of ConfigMap entirely. ConfigMap is explicitly designed for non sensitive configuration, and the very next topic covers the dedicated object built specifically for sensitive data instead.

Version control every ConfigMap manifest alongside the rest of the application's Kubernetes manifests, treating configuration changes with the exact same review discipline already applied to code changes throughout this course.

Group related configuration values into logically organized ConfigMaps rather than one enormous, catch all ConfigMap holding every setting for an entire application, improving both readability and the ability to update pieces independently.

Choose the consumption method, environment variables, volume mounts, or command arguments, deliberately based on the application's own configuration style, rather than defaulting reflexively to whichever method was used most recently elsewhere.

blocks.content: The Single Most Valuable Takeaway

ConfigMap is the foundational mechanism that keeps container images environment agnostic, letting the exact same tested, versioned image run correctly across development, staging, and production, each supplying its own distinct configuration values.

Its three consumption methods, environment variables, volume mounts, and command arguments, each fit a different application configuration style, and the next several topics in this module give each one the full depth needed to use it confidently.

The next topic, Secrets, covers the direct counterpart to ConfigMap built specifically for sensitive data, sharing much of the same API shape while handling the one critical difference that matters most: genuine sensitivity.

Keep the environment agnostic image principle firmly in mind. Every configuration decision in this module should be measured against one question: does this keep the image itself free of anything specific to a single environment.

One final, practical reminder before moving on: a ConfigMap is only ever appropriate for non sensitive data, and the next topic exists specifically to give sensitive data the different handling it genuinely requires.
ConfigMap is now fully covered; Secrets, its direct counterpart for sensitive data, follows immediately next.

blocks.title: ConfigMap In Full
points: ConfigMap stores non sensitive configuration data as key value pairs, kept separate from the container image, letting the same image run unchanged across every environment.
It can be consumed by a Pod as environment variables, as mounted files, or as command line arguments, each suited to a different application configuration style.
ConfigMap manifests should be version controlled and reviewed with the same discipline applied to application code, and sensitive values never belong in a ConfigMap.
A practical size limit, around one megabyte, and namespace scoping are both worth understanding when structuring configuration for a real, multi environment application.
Secrets, covered next, is the direct counterpart to ConfigMap, sharing much of its API shape while handling genuinely sensitive configuration data.
